paper_title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Scientific discovery has long driven human progress, enabling advances across chemistry, biology, and medicine. Central to this process is identifying scientific principles that govern the systems of interest. In complex scientific discovery processes such as drug discovery, the scientific principles are usually unknown due to the complexity of the underlying systems. Therefore, empirical principles are usually constructed from progressively accumulated experimental observations during test-time discovery to explain causality between input characteristics and experimental outcomes (Scheiner & Willig, 2008; Hone et al., 2015; Pearlstein et al., 2021). Specifically, hypotheses that explain specific scope of individual observations are formed and then generalized into principles that cover broader scope of observations, being formulated as hypotheses-to-principle construction pipeline (Lamma et al., 2000; Kakas & Michael, 2020; Engelschalt et al., 2023). However, constructing such principles by human researchers requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, creating bottleneck in scientific discovery. As illustrated in Fig. 1, human researchers also follow the hypotheses-to-principle construction pipeline, while leveraging an extensive body of prior knowledge. They interpret the experimental observations, hypothesize the plausible causal relationships, generalize them by analyzing the recurring patterns, and revise hypotheses when new observations contradict prior explanations. As experimental observations accumulate, researchers formulate tentative explanations of individual outcomes, generalize recurring relationships across observations into scientific principles, and reassess these explanations in light of new observations. The resulting principles guide further investigation, forming an iterative discovery cycle. However, this process requires substantial domain expertise, time, labor, and financial resources, limiting the pace of scientific discovery. scientific principles. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) (Anthropic, 2026; OpenAI, 2026a;b; Xu et al., 2026) have motivated growing efforts to automate scientific research (AI4Science & Quantum, 2023), including idea generation (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Baek et al., 2025), experimental design (Gottweis et al., 2026; Schmidgall et al., 2026), and candidate optimization (Wang et al., 2025a;b; Roohani et al., 2025; Ran et al., 2025). Despite these advances, constructing and continually refining principles for scientific discovery from progressively accumulated experimental observations remains underexplored. In this work, we explore the test-time construction of empirical principles that explain how input characteristics contribute to observed outcomes using LLMs. However, operationalizing this process presents two challenges. First, an individual input and its observed outcome provide limited guidance for an LLM to distinguish among possible explanations. Multiple input characteristics can account for the same outcome, making it difficult to identify which factors to emphasize when generating hypothesis. Hypothesis generation therefore requires evidence that helps narrow the range of possible explanations. Second, the observations accumulated during discovery cover only small fraction of the vast space of scientific inputs. LLM-generated hypotheses based on this limited coverage can provide incomplete or incorrect explanations for other inputs, and these limitations can carry over into the principles constructed from them. As new observations accumulate, they can expose these limitations, making it necessary to reassess and revise earlier hypotheses. To address these challenges, we propose PRINCIPIA, an LLM-based hypotheses-to-principle construction framework that inductively derives principles from progressively accumulated experimental observations during test-time discovery. Drawing on how human researchers develop scientific knowledge, PRINCIPIA consists of three key components: (i) comparative causal hypothesis generation, (ii) inductive principle construction, and (iii) hypothesis revision via new observations. Specifically, for hypothesis generation, PRINCIPIA compares related inputs and their experimental outcomes rather than single observation to formulate causal hypotheses, narrowing the factors considered to their shared and differing characteristics. For principle construction, it groups related inputs and inductively combines recurring relationships across their hypotheses into principles. These hypotheses and principles guide subsequent prediction or optimization through retrieval, getting new observations. Finally, new observations are used to revise the used hypotheses and reconstruct the resulting principles, allowing the knowledge to evolve during test-time discovery. We evaluate PRINCIPIA on extensive benchmarks of scientific discovery tasks, spanning molecular, protein, and gene optimization, as well as molecular property prediction. Our results demonstrate that PRINCIPIA outperforms baselines that rely on internal knowledge, experience summaries, or external knowledge, demonstrating the effectiveness of test-time construction of hypotheses and principles. Further analyses show that PRINCIPIA achieves comparable optimization performance with 55% reduction in experimental budget compared with an experience-summary baseline, demonstrating its cost-effectiveness in scientific optimization. Qualitative analyses show that the constructed hypotheses capture relationships between inputs and experimental outcomes, while the induced principles are consistent with scientific literature. These results show that constructing empirical principles at test time can improve both the effectiveness and efficiency of scientific discovery.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Automated Scientific Discovery and Optimization Advances in machine learning have emerged as powerful tools for automating scientific discovery, ranging from systems that assist individual stages, such as hypothesis and idea generation (Wang et al., 2024; Vasu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Baek et al., 2025), to end-to-end AI scientists (Schmidgall et al., 2025; 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Gottweis et al., 2026) that formulate research proposals, conduct experiments, and generate scientific papers with minimal human supervision. While these works seek to automate the broader research workflow, another line of research focuses on discovering novel scientific candidates with minimal prior context. For example, Bagal et al. (2021); Xu et al. (2022); Lee et al. (2023); Watson et al. (2023) develop deep generative models that explore latent spaces to identify promising candidates by learning representations of the underlying scientific domains. Meanwhile, with the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs), agentic approaches for candidate generation by LLMs have been developed (M. Bran et al., 2024; Roohani et al., 2025). Building on this direction, recent approaches leverage the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, using them as surrogate operators in Evolutionary Algorithms (Holland, 1962) to guide exploration of vast search spaces through iterative generation and evolutionary search (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a;b; Novikov et al., 2025; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026; Lange et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a) across diverse scientific research domains. Despite their progress, constructing reusable scientific knowledge from experimental observations during discovery remains underexplored. Our work addresses this gap by dynamically constructing reusable causal principles at test time, enabling more informed discovery. Knowledge-Augmented Scientific Discovery Building on the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020), growing body of work has incorporated external knowledge into scientific discovery systems. These approaches include leveraging existing literature to generate open-ended hypotheses and research proposals through multi-agent systems (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Baek et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), incorporating external knowledge bases into the discovery loop to inform experimental decisions (Boiko et al., 2023; M. Bran et al., 2024; Roohani et al., 2025), and employing deep-search agents to retrieve promising research directions (Liu et al., 2025). Recent work has also explored using experience during discovery to guide subsequent exploration. For instance, Pu et al. (2025) balance exploration and exploitation over pre-configured high-quality scientific knowledge to guide subsequent optimization of both candidates and principles, while Ran et al. (2025) summarize characteristics of previously discovered candidates into single document. Another line of works leverages predictive strategies for machine learning research (Jiang et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026) or constructs offline memories from heterogeneous tasks for future reuse (Zhang et al., 2026b; Yao et al., 2026). Beyond retrieving literature or reusing summarized experience, our work focuses on causal principle induction from observations accumulated during test-time discovery. Rather than using these observations solely to guide subsequent actions, we develop explicit hypotheses about how input characteristics may contribute to observed outcomes and generalize recurring relationships into principles.

sections.title: 3 PRINCIPIA: TEST-TIME HYPOTHESES TO PRINCIPLE CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: We present PRINCIPIA, an LLM-based framework that constructs and refines empirical principles at test time by forming and generalizing hypotheses from progressively accumulated experimental observations  (Fig. 2)  . We first introduce comparative causal hypotheses formed from related inputs and their observed outcomes, inductive principle construction that generalizes recurring patterns across these hypotheses, and hypotheses revision that applies the constructed hypotheses and principles to get new observations and updates the previously formed hypotheses via new observations. Task Settings We consider two central tasks in scientific discovery: optimization and prediction. Let denote scientific input, such as molecule, and let denote an experimental oracle that returns an observed property or characteristic O(x). We refer to this outcome as scientific observation, which could be categorical label or numerical measurement. In the optimization task, the goal is to find an optimal instance that best achieves specified scientific objective such as maximizing desired property, through successive modifications. Given an input x, the action is to propose modified input x, which is evaluated by the experimental oracle to obtain the observation O(x). In the prediction task, the goal is to predict property or characteristic of given input x.

sections.title: 3.1 COMPARATIVE CAUSAL HYPOTHESIS
sections.content: We now turn to the first step of our scientific knowledge construction, which is the formation of causal hypotheses. The goal of hypothesis formation is to propose explicit explanations of the factors that have contributed to an observed experimental outcome. However, an individual input and its observed outcome alone generally provide limited evidence for distinguishing the contributions of different input characteristics. To provide more reliable basis for hypothesis formation, we construct comparative evidence by combining related inputs with their corresponding observed outcomes. From this evidence, we generate comparative causal hypothesis, defined as tentative explanation of how similarities and differences between two inputs account for their observed outcomes. Comparative Evidence To narrow the scope of comparison, we first form comparative evidence which consists of two similar inputs and their experimental outcomes. Specifically, we compose reference-to-target comparisons xi xj from the available experimental data, = {(xi, O(xi))}N i=1, by selecting related inputs in the sense that they share similar input characteristics. In the optimization task, we compare generated candidate xj with the input xi from which it was derived, using their observed outcomes to examine the effects of the modification. In the prediction task, such modification histories are not generally available, so we compute the pairwise distances between each target input xj and nearby reference inputs xi from D. To compute the pairwise distances, we leverage domain-appropriate distance measures, such as fingerprint-based distance for molecules, and select references with the smallest distances, regardless of whether their observed labels match the targets label. In both settings, each pair provides comparative evidence consisting of both inputs and their observations: eij = (cid:0)xi, O(xi), xj, O(xj)(cid:1). sections.title: INDUCTIVE PRINCIPLE
sections.content: Even though each comparative causal hypothesis provides tentative explanation grounded in particular pair of inputs, single hypothesis could depend on characteristics specific to those inputs, failing to model the general underlying scientific principles. Inspired by the human scientific process where the scientist generalizes from specific observations to broader principles, we construct inductive principles that summarize recurring relationships between input characteristics and observed outcomes across multiple comparisons. Similarity-based Clustering We first group the inputs represented by nodes in Mh to examine recurring patterns among inputs with similar characteristics by applying k-medoids clustering with the domain-specific pairwise distances. Let Gk denote the set of input indices in the k-th cluster and Ah denote the directed edge set of the hypothesis graph Mh. For each cluster, we collect the comparative evidence and causal hypotheses on all edges incident to its members: Ek = {(eij, Hij) (i, j) Ah, Gk Gk}. This grouping brings together inputs with similar characteristics and the hypotheses associated with their comparisons, providing basis for identifying recurring relationships across observations. Principle Induction For each cluster, an LLM inductively infers compact principle based on (cid:0)Ek; q(cid:1). The model identifies recurring its associated evidence and hypotheses: Pk = LLMprinciple relationships across the associated causal hypotheses and generalizes them into causal principle. By integrating these across multiple comparisons, this process extends beyond individual observations to derive causal principle that captures more general relationships. We store each principle with its associated cluster in principle memory Mp = {(Gk, Pk)}K k=1, organizing the induced principles into more general level of scientific knowledge.

sections.title: 3.3 HYPOTHESIS REVISION VIA NEW OBSERVATIONS
sections.content: Thus far, we have described how to generate comparative causal hypotheses and inductive principles from experimental observations: the inductive principles are constructed from comparative causal hypotheses, making the reliability of these principles dependent on the hypotheses underlying them. However, experimental observations cover only small fraction of the space of possible inputs, and hypotheses formed from this limited evidence can overlook factors relevant to other inputs. These limitations can also affect the principles constructed from them, leading to potentially inaccurate or incomplete conclusions. Therefore, we revise hypotheses to enhance their reliability and improve the quality of the principles constructed from them. Specifically, inspired by how scientists validate existing hypotheses through further investigation, we use the generated hypotheses and principles to guide further task-specific predictions or candidate generation, obtaining additional experimental observations. We then revise the hypotheses using new observations, either by comparing predictions with observed labels or by examining the evaluated outcomes of generated candidates. Hypothesis Application and Revision To obtain new observations for hypothesis revision, we first retrieve relevant hypotheses and principles and apply them to new inputs. Given query input x, we first construct hypothesis and principle candidate pools drawn from Mh and Mp, and then leverage an LLM-based retrieval, where an LLM that can handle long-context inputs independently selects kh hypotheses Rh(x) and kp principles Rp(x) from candidate pools, respectively, based on their relevance to the query and task description. The selected knowledge guides the task-specific action such as optimization or prediction, after which the corresponding observations are obtained by these actions. For more details on the retrieval and application of knowledge, please refer to Appendix A. We then revise the hypotheses retrieved and used during the current round. For each selected hypothesis Hij, we construct new observation Bij by sampling new observations from that round together with their associated inputs and outcomes. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: We evaluate PRINCIPIA on scientific discovery tasks including scientific optimization tasks spanning molecules, proteins, and genes, as well as molecular property prediction. We provide implementation details in Appendix and the algorithmic workflow for optimization and prediction in Appendix D.

sections.title: 4.1 SCIENTIFIC OPTIMIZATION
sections.content: Experimental Setting We evaluate PRINCIPIA on scientific optimization tasks under restricted oracle budget spanning molecules, proteins, and genes from the Scientific Discovery Evaluation benchmark (Song et al., 2025), involving designing molecules with desired properties (Gao et al., 2022), optimizing protein sequences for target functions (Wang et al., 2025b), and identifying gene perturbations that produce desired cellular responses (Schmidt et al., 2022; Scharenberg et al., 2023). We report AUC@10 to measure optimization progress over oracle evaluations and the average oracle scores of the top 100 molecules or top 50 protein sequences. For gene perturbation, we additionally report hit ratio following Roohani et al. (2025). To ensure fair comparisons across variants, we normalize the fitness values of common variants for the Syn-3bfo, Scharenberg22, and IFNG tasks to the range [0, 1] when computing AUC. We use GPT-5-mini (Singh et al., 2025) as the backbone. We provide task-specific objectives, the application of PRINCIPIA, search budgets, and evaluation protocols in Appendix B. Baselines We compare against MolLEO (Wang et al., 2025a), an optimizer without guidance, ExLLM (Ran et al., 2025) which guides optimization by an evolving textual summary from experience, WebSearch which provides guidance retrieved from the web, DeepEvolve (Liu et al., 2025) which uses web search guidance based on the optimization experience, and PiFlow (Pu et al., 2025) which guides optimization without observation-guided causal hypotheses. For molecular optimization, we additionally include REINVENT (Olivecrona et al., 2017), reinforcement learning method for molecular generation, Augmented Memory (Guo & Schwaller, 2023) which enhances reinforcement learning through experience replay, and Graph GA (Jensen, 2019) which applies genetic operations to molecular graphs. We provide implementation details and configurations in Appendix C.1. Results As shown in Tables 1 and 2, PRINCIPIA consistently outperforms baseline without guidance (MolLEO), demonstrating that constructing task-specific knowledge is beneficial for guiding optimization. PRINCIPIA also outperforms baselines that use experience summaries (ExLLM), showing that constructing structured knowledge including causal hypotheses and inductive principles is more effective than textual summary of past observations. Notably, PRINCIPIA also outperforms baselines that use external knowledge (WebSearch, DeepEvolve), indicating that constructing taskspecific knowledge at test-time provides core information to achieve the optimization objective, while external knowledge is less relevant to the specific task. sections.title: 4.2 MOLECULAR PROPERTY PREDICTION
sections.content: Experimental Setting We evaluate PRINCIPIA on molecular property prediction with eight binary classification tasks from TDC (Huang et al., 2021): four toxicity-related tasks (DILI, hERG, Ames, and Skin Reaction) and four CYP inhibition tasks (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4). We use scaffold split to construct held-out test set containing molecular scaffolds absent from the training set. To simulate the test-time scenario for prediction tasks, we equally split the training dataset and construct knowledge by progressively observing the labels of each subset. After constructing knowledge from the training dataset, we evaluate the resulting knowledge on the held-out test set, whose labels are excluded from knowledge construction and revision. We use GPT-5.4-mini as the backbone. We report accuracy and macro-F1, averaged over three random seeds. We provide details on data preparation, round construction, and evaluation protocols in Appendix B.2. Baselines We compare against Direct prediction which predicts without additional context, and Fewshot prediction which conditions predictions on examples from the whole training dataset composed of input molecules and their labels. We further consider Textual summary which summarizes sequentially observed training examples into texts, Internal principles which provides principles generated from the LLMs internal knowledge, and External principles which provides principles retrieved from web. We further provide implementation details and configurations in Appendix C.2. Results As shown in Table 3, PRINCIPIA consistently outperforms all baselines across eight molecular property prediction tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of constructing hypotheses and principles for molecular property prediction. In particular, its improvements over few-shot prediction suggest that organizing observations into explicit causal hypotheses and principles provides more effective guidance than supplying labeled examples alone. Table 4 shows that providing these hypotheses improves performance over the optimizer without hypothesis guidance, indicating that explicit hypotheses about the relationships between input characteristics and observed outcomes provide useful guidance for subsequent optimization. We also compare comparative hypothesis generation with non-comparative variant that generates each hypothesis from single input and its observed outcome (w/o comparative). Evaluation Budget Efficiency Scientific experiments can be costly, making it important to reach desired outcomes with fewer evaluations. We therefore examine whether the constructed causal principles help reduce this evaluation burden under an extended oracle budget. As shown in Fig. 5, PRINCIPIA achieves the best final performance among the compared methods. Surprisingly, PRINCIPIA matches the final performance of ExLLM, WebSearch, MolLEO, and DeepEvolve with approximately 55%, 84%, 86%, and 86% fewer oracle evaluations, respectively. These results suggest that constructing task-specific knowledge can reduce the number of evaluations required for discovery, potentially lowering the cost of experimental investigation. Effect of Knowledge Retrieval In our framework, knowledge retrieval plays central role: knowledge retrieval determines which hypotheses guide subsequent actions and are later revisited in light of new observations. To examine its contribution, we ablate the LLM-based selection. As shown in Fig. 6, removing this lowers performance, suggesting that query-dependent selection helps identify useful knowledge for subsequent investigation, through which the selected hypotheses can be reassessed against new observations. Notably, removing LLM-based retrieval yields an AUC@10 of 0.364, comparable to 0.374 obtained without hypothesis revision in Fig. 4, suggesting that selecting relevant knowledge is important for realizing the benefits of hypothesis revision during optimization. Qualitative Analysis We further qualitatively analyze the constructed hypotheses and principles to examine their reasonableness and scientific plausibility. As shown in Table 5, for pairs with the same labels, the hypotheses propose possible explanation based on the shared structures. If the labels differ, they propose structural differences that may account for the contrasting outcomes. The induced principle provides broader view by generalizing this explanation across related comparisons, identifying recurring motifs (i.e., epoxide) while distinguishing specific structure (i.e., aminoalcohol) that lacks relevant property (i.e., strained electrophile). Interestingly, this principle is consistent with prior studies linking epoxide-containing compounds to mutagenicity (Seiler, 1984; Rosman et al., 1988). This result shows how comparative hypotheses provide reasonable explanations for observed outcomes, while the induced principle captures scientifically plausible relationships across related molecules. An additional qualitative example of hypothesis revision is provided in Appendix E.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied the test-time construction of empirical principles for scientific discovery, focusing on how progressively accumulated observations can be transformed into knowledge that guides further investigation. To address this problem, we proposed PRINCIPIA, an LLM-based framework that forms comparative causal hypotheses, generalizes recurring relationships into inductive principles,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: and uses new observations to revise the hypotheses and reconstruct the principles. Experiments spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction demonstrate that PRINCIPIA outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, experience summaries, or external knowledge, with further analyses supporting its efficiency in reducing oracle evaluations and plausibility of the constructed principles. We believe our work highlights test-time hypotheses-to-principle construction as an important direction for advancing LLM-based scientific discovery, enabling accumulated observations to continually inform subsequent investigation.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS OF PRINCIPIA
sections.content: Comparative Evidence and Hypothesis Generation For scientific optimization, we form reference-to-target comparisons from the inputs used in candidate generation to the resulting evaluated candidates. Each comparison provides comparative evidence containing both inputs and their scientific observations, expressed as oracle scores, from which the LLM generates comparative causal hypotheses. For molecular property prediction, we pair each newly observed target molecule with up to three reference molecules ranked by Tanimoto similarity (Willett et al., 1998), excluding the target itself. The reference pool contains the molecules observed in previous rounds and those whose labels have become available in the current round. Reference selection does not filter by label, so comparisons can involve either matching or differing observations. For each reference-to-target comparison, we store the comparative evidence and its associated hypotheses as hypothesis record (eij, Hij) in Mh. record may contain multiple hypotheses explaining the same comparison. Molecular inputs are represented as SMILES (Weininger, 1988), protein inputs as amino-acid sequences, and gene inputs as HGNC1 gene symbols. The task-specific hypothesis-generation prompts are provided in Appendix F. Similarity-based Clustering and Principle Induction We group the inputs represented by nodes in Mh using soft-balanced k-medoids with domain-specific pairwise distances. For molecules, we compute Tanimoto distance from 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints with radius 2. For protein sequences, we use normalized Hamming distance for equal-length sequences and Jaccard distance between sets of overlapping amino-acid 3-mers for unequal-length sequences. For genes, we embed the gene symbols using text-embedding-3-large (OpenAI, 2024), normalize the embeddings to unit length, and use cosine distance. The hypothesis memory retains inputs and their associated observations, including initial inputs without hypothesis edges. In optimization, clustering uses the highest-scoring input nodes in Mh, corresponding to the current population. In prediction, it uses all observed molecules represented in Mh. For inputs, we set the number of clusters to max(1, n/10), targeting ten inputs per cluster. We use size-balancing penalty of 0.01, minimum and maximum cluster sizes of 5 and 15. For each cluster, we collect the comparative evidence and associated hypotheses linked to its members. An LLM then inductively infers principle by generalizing recurring relationships across these hypotheses while accounting for conflicting observations. We store each inductive principle with its associated cluster in Mp. The task-specific principle-induction prompts are provided in Appendix F. Knowledge Retrieval We independently retrieve hypothesis records from Mh and inductive principles from Mp by first constructing candidate pools and then using an LLM to select knowledge relevant to the query input and task description. For hypothesis retrieval in optimization, we rank hypothesis records by the fitness difference between the reference and target inputs. We then alternate between the largest improvements and declines, selecting up to 100 unique records. For prediction, we rank hypothesis records by the Tanimoto similarity between each records target molecule and the query. We then select up to 50 records with matching reference and target labels and 50 with different labels. The LLM receives this candidate pool and selects relevant hypothesis records, each containing comparative evidence and its associated hypotheses. To construct the principle candidate pool, we rank clusters by their maximum member similarity to the query using the domain-specific similarity corresponding to the pairwise distance above, retain at most 100 clusters, and ask the LLM to select relevant inductive principles. The optimization configuration retrieves up to three hypothesis records and one principle per query. In prediction, the number of retrieved hypothesis records is configurable, while the LLM determines how many principles to select. The retrieved knowledge is provided as textual context for the task-specific action: candidate generation or property prediction. The task-specific retrieval prompts are provided in Appendix F. Hypothesis Revision via New Observations We revise the hypotheses retrieved and used during the current generation or prediction round. For each selected hypothesis record, we uniformly sample up to five new observations from that generation or round. In optimization, the sampled observations 1https://www.genenames.org/

sections.content: include input pairs (x, x) and their observed outcomes (O(x), O(x)). In prediction, they include query molecules x, their predictions ˆO(x), and their observed labels O(x). The LLM receives the original comparative evidence, the current hypotheses, the sampled new observations, and the task description, and can retain, revise, remove, or add hypotheses. We update the hypotheses in the corresponding records in Mh while retaining their original comparative evidence. The task-specific hypothesis-revision prompts are provided in Appendix F. TASK-SPECIFIC EXPERIMENTAL SETTINGS This section describes the datasets, the application of PRINCIPIA to each task, and the experimental configurations. B.1 SCIENTIFIC OPTIMIZATION We use GPT-5-mini-2025-08-07 (Singh et al., 2025) as the backbone model for scientific optimization, with temperature set to 1.0. We report mean results over three random seeds. Shared Procedure for Scientific Optimization PRINCIPIA, MolLEO, ExLLM, WebSearch, and DeepEvolve share population-based optimization architecture based on MolLEO (Wang et al., 2025a) and the implementation of Song et al. (2025). For optimization, we maintain population consisting of the highest-scoring distinct inputs in the accumulated experimental records D. We sample mating pool from according to normalized fitness, handling negative scores before converting them into selection probabilities. Following Song et al. (2025), the mating-pool size equals the offspring budget per generation. The task-specific operations are described below. When the LLM proposes multiple candidates, we select the first valid, previously unevaluated candidate, falling back to the first valid candidate if all proposals are duplicates. Previously evaluated inputs reuse their recorded scores. Newly evaluated inputs are added to D, from which the population for the next generation is selected. Knowledge Update Schedule of PRINCIPIA PRINCIPIA starts optimization with empty hypothesis and principle memories, so the first generation proceeds without retrieved guidance. After candidate evaluation, we generate comparative causal hypotheses from the reference-to-target comparisons and their observed outcomes. From the second generation onward, we also revise the hypotheses retrieved and used during that generation using its new observations. We then reconstruct inductive principles from the updated hypotheses and population, making the resulting memories available for candidate generation in the next generation. B.1.1 MOLECULAR OPTIMIZATION Datasets and Objectives We evaluate five tasks from the Practical Molecule Optimization (PMO) benchmark (Gao et al., 2022): JNK3, GSK3β, Median1, Median2, and Valsartan SMARTS. JNK3 and GSK3β reward predicted inhibitory activity against their respective targets. Median1 and Median2 measure simultaneous similarity to two reference molecules: camphor and menthol for Median1, and tadalafil and sildenafil for Median2. Valsartan SMARTS combines target-substructure requirement with physicochemical property objectives. We use the benchmark scoring functions as experimental oracles, with higher scores indicating better satisfaction of the objective. We adopt the task descriptions and objectives available in Wang et al. (2025a); for the remaining task, we follow Ran et al. (2025) and match the instruction style. Task Execution and Application of PRINCIPIA Each generation applies rule-based crossover to selected parent pairs, followed by LLM-based mutation. Before each mutation call, we use the crossover product as the query input and provide the retrieved hypotheses and principles in the mutation prompt. Both crossover products and mutated offspring are evaluated by the experimental oracle. We form reference-to-target comparisons from each parent to its crossover product and from the crossover product to its mutated offspring. Each comparison includes both inputs and their observed outcomes as comparative evidence for the generation-end knowledge update. The five tasks share this execution process, with their respective task descriptions and oracles determining the optimization objective. The prompts are provided in Appendix F.1.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Experimental Configuration and Evaluation Each run starts from pre-sampled population of 200 molecules drawn randomly from the ZINC (Irwin & Shoichet, 2005) pool, shared across corresponding methods. We generate up to 100 offspring per generation and use budget of 1,000 distinct oracle evaluations, including initialization. We report AUC@10, the area under the trajectory of the mean score of the ten best molecules observed so far, following Gao et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2025a). We evaluate this trajectory every 100 oracle calls, apply trapezoidal integration, and normalize by the evaluation budget. We also report Avg@100, the mean oracle score of the 100 highest-scoring evaluated molecules. B.1.2 PROTEIN SEQUENCE ENGINEERING Datasets and Objectives We evaluate Syn-3bfo, AAV, and GB1 using the task-specific fitness oracles provided by the protein optimization benchmark (Wang et al., 2025b). Syn-3bfo uses synthetic fitness landscape derived from Potts model, AAV uses pretrained convolutional predictor of capsid fitness, and GB1 uses experimentally measured fitness values through sequence lookup table. We follow the corresponding oracle implementations for score normalization. Each task maximizes its fitness objective over amino-acid sequences of the task-specific length using the 20 standard amino acids. We construct task descriptions from these objectives, as the original benchmark does not provide task-specific optimization prompts. Task Execution and Application of PRINCIPIA We apply length-preserving uniform crossover to selected parent sequences, followed by LLM-based mutation under the task-specific sequence constraints. The crossover sequence serves as the query input, and the retrieved hypotheses and principles are supplied to the mutation prompt. As in molecular optimization, we retain both the intermediate crossover sequences and the mutated offspring with their observed outcomes. We form reference-to-target comparisons from each parent to its crossover sequence and from the crossover sequence to its mutated offspring, providing comparative evidence for the generation-end knowledge update. Syn-3bfo, AAV, and GB1 share this process while using their respective task descriptions, sequence constraints, and fitness oracles. The prompts are provided in Appendix F.2. Experimental Configuration and Evaluation Each run starts from 48 pre-sampled sequences, including the wild-type sequence, and generates up to 48 offspring per generation. Corresponding methods share the initial population, and the budget is 200 distinct oracle evaluations, including initialization. We compute AUC@10 from the mean fitness of the ten best sequences observed so far, using an evaluation frequency of 100 oracle calls and trapezoidal integration normalized by the evaluation budget. For Syn-3bfo, fitness values are normalized to [0, 1] before computing AUC, using common normalization across methods. We also report Avg@50, the mean fitness of the 50 highest-scoring evaluated sequences. B.1.3 GENE PERTURBATION Datasets and Objectives We evaluate Scharenberg22 and IFNG using the CRISPR-screen datasets and task definitions adopted by BioDiscoveryAgent (Roohani et al., 2025). Inputs are gene symbols, and the oracle returns score derived from the recorded perturbation effect. Scharenberg22 concerns lysosomal choline recycling (Scharenberg et al., 2023), and we maximize its recorded screen score. IFNG concerns regulation of interferon-γ production in human cells, and we maximize the absolute recorded effect, rewarding both strong increases and strong decreases. IFNG has larger gene search space than Scharenberg22. We reuse the benchmark task descriptions. Task Execution and Application of PRINCIPIA Given pair of selected genes and their scores, the LLM directly proposes another gene to evaluate, without separate crossover operation. We use the selected genes as query inputs to retrieve hypotheses and principles for the proposal prompt. Previously proposed genes are also included to reduce duplicate proposals. The proposed gene is evaluated using its recorded perturbation effect. We form reference-to-target comparison from each selected gene to the proposed gene, retaining both inputs and their observed outcomes as comparative evidence for the generation-end knowledge update. Scharenberg22 and IFNG share this process, with their respective objectives and gene search spaces. The prompts are provided in Appendix F.3.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Experimental Configuration and Evaluation We use pre-sampled initial populations of 32 genes for Scharenberg22 and 128 for IFNG, with matching offspring budgets. The oracle budgets are 192 and 768 distinct genes, respectively, corresponding to 160 and 640 newly proposed genes beyond initialization, following Roohani et al. (2025). We compute AUC@10 from the mean score of the ten best genes observed so far, after normalizing scores to [0, 1] using common normalization across methods for each dataset. The trajectory is evaluated every 100 oracle calls and integrated with the trapezoidal rule, then normalized by the evaluation budget. We also report Hit Ratio, the fraction of benchmark hit genes recovered among the distinct newly proposed genes. Hit Ratio excludes the initial population and measures recall rather than the fraction of proposed genes that are hits. We report the unfiltered hit sets in Table 2 and an additional evaluation excluding essential genes in Table 7. Previously proposed genes are supplied to all LLM-based baselines to reduce duplicate proposals; the additional PiFlow-specific handling is described in Appendix C.1. B.2 MOLECULAR PROPERTY PREDICTION We use gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17 as the backbone model for molecular property prediction, with temperature set to 1.0. We report mean results over three random seeds. Datasets and Objectives We evaluate eight binary classification tasks from Therapeutics Data Commons (Huang et al., 2021). The toxicity-related tasks are DILI, hERG, Ames, and Skin Reaction, which concern liver injury, hERG channel blockade, mutagenicity, and skin reaction, respectively. The remaining tasks predict inhibition of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4. Each task predicts molecules label from its SMILES and task description. Task Execution and Application of PRINCIPIA We construct knowledge over successive rounds in which new molecular observations become available. The first round reveals labels to initialize the hypothesis and principle memories, without prediction or revision. In each subsequent round, we retrieve hypotheses and principles for each newly introduced query molecule and provide them as context for label prediction, keeping that molecules observed label hidden. After the rounds predictions are complete, we reveal the labels and revise the hypotheses used during prediction using the resulting new observations. We then generate comparative causal hypotheses for the newly labeled molecules and reconstruct inductive principles before proceeding to the next round. After the final round, the memories are fixed and used for held-out test prediction without further updates. All eight datasets follow this schedule with their respective task descriptions and labels. The prompts are provided in Appendix F.4. Experimental Configuration and Evaluation We prepare training, validation, and test partitions using scaffold splitting and randomly sample up to 200 training molecules and 50 test molecules per class for each run. The training molecules are divided into six rounds, with each molecule appearing once. We retrieve up to three hypothesis records per prediction. The validation partition is not used in sequential knowledge construction, and held-out test labels are excluded from hypothesis generation, revision, and principle construction. We evaluate the fixed memories using accuracy and macro-F1, the unweighted mean of the class-specific F1 scores. Responses without valid task label are treated as incorrect predictions and remain in the evaluation set.

sections.title: C BASELINES
sections.content: C.1 SCIENTIFIC OPTIMIZATION REINVENT We restrict our evaluation of the reinforcement-learning-based REINVENT algorithm to the pre-implemented code from the open-source official PMO (Gao et al., 2022) repository2. We adopt the default hyperparameters listed in the official code repository. Specifically, the agent policy is optimized with learning rate of 0.0005 and batch size of 64 molecules sampled per update. The reward-scaling coefficient sigma is set to 500, and the experience-replay parameter is set to 24, specifying the number of previously seen high-scoring molecules that are re-sampled from prioritized memory and added to each update to reinforce promising candidates. We set the maximum number of oracle calls to 1000 and the patience to 10, with patience threshold of 1e-3, and 2https://github.com/wenhao-gao/mol_opt.git

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: AUC computation frequency value to 100, matching the experimental setting of PRINCIPIA and its LLM-based discovery baselines. Augmented Memory We additionally evaluate optimization algorithms with Augmented Memory, reinforced extension of REINVENT that introduces memory augmentation. Our implementation follows the official PMO repository. Consistent with the REINVENT protocol, we cap the maximum number of oracle calls at 1,000 and use patience of 10 with threshold of 1e-3, evaluating AUC every 100 oracle calls. As with REINVENT, we retain the default hyperparameters hard-coded in the official repository: batch size of 64, sigma of 500, replay-buffer size of 1,000, learning rate of 5e-4, and 2 augmentation rounds per augmented-memory update. Graph GA Likewise, as with other machine-learning-based optimization algorithms, we follow the implementation details provided in the official PMO repository. We set the maximum number of oracle calls to 1,000, the patience to 10, with patience threshold of 1e-3, and the AUC evaluation frequency to 100, consistent with the settings used by other machine-learning-based molecular optimization methods. Since Graph GA is population-based evolutionary search method, we use the same pre-sampled initial population as PRINCIPIA and the other baselines, consisting of 200 samples. We additionally set the offspring population size to 100 to align its hyperparameter settings with those used for PRINCIPIA. For the mutation rate, we follow the default configuration in the official repository and set it to 0.067. MolLEO We reimplement MolLEO based on its original implementation (Wang et al., 2025a)3 and the implementation of Song et al. (2025)4. It provides the shared optimization architecture described in Appendix B.1, using crossover followed by LLM mutation for molecules and protein sequences and direct LLM-based proposals for gene perturbation. MolLEO uses this architecture without the hypothesis and principle guidance supplied by PRINCIPIA. Its oracle budget, population settings, patience, and convergence threshold are matched to PRINCIPIA. ExLLM Following the experience-guided memory mechanism of ExLLM (Ran et al., 2025) implemented in the official repository5, our textual-memory baseline augments the MolLEO baseline with an experience summarization mechanism. Once per generation, after more than 100 candidates have been evaluated, an LLM analyzes 10 sampled high-performing and 10 low-performing candidates from top-100 candidates based on scalar fitness to distill rolling, 200-word naturallanguage experience summary. The newly generated summary is integrated with the previous summary and injected into each generation-level LLM call with probability 0.5, using ExLLMs experience-injection wrapper and analysis instructions. Since ExLLMs base implementation targets multi-objective optimization setting, whereas our evaluation optimizes single scalar objective, we adapt its candidate-summarization procedure to account for this mismatch in the optimization setting. Specifically, we describe each candidate using its scalar fitness value together with taskspecific description prompt, rather than an explicit listing of multiple objective values. All remaining optimization hyperparameters are kept identical to those used by PRINCIPIA. PiFlow Since no official implementation is publicly available, we reimplement PiFlow (Pu et al., 2025) following the original paper. We retain its Min-Max principle scoring, score-based Refine/Validate/Explore procedure, and round-robin group-chat protocol, using the default hyperparameters λ = 0.5, = 3, and = 10 without tuning. We minimally adapt the Planner and Hypothesis prompts to our experimental settings, replace the Experiment agent with deterministic oracle, and use the same backbone LLM as PRINCIPIA. We use text-embedding-3-large (OpenAI, 2024) for semantic novelty and initialize three principles using the papers cold-start procedure, due to the absence of pre-configured principles in our experimental setting. At each LLM call, we generate three candidates and evaluate the first valid candidate without explicit duplicate checking, matching original papers intent for generating single candidate based on single hypothesis. For molecular optimization and protein sequence engineering, we follow the papers 24-iteration short-horizon protocol, including the cold-start iteration, and evaluate top-k fitness and AUC over de-duplicated candidates. For gene perturbation, we instead match the oracle-call budgets of PRINCIPIA and other baselines (768 and 192) and compute the metric (hit-ratio) over the resulting distinct candidates. 3https://github.com/zoom-wang112358/MOLLEO 4https://github.com/HowieHwong/sde-harness 5https://github.com/HuskyNian/ExLLM

sections.content: DeepEvolve We adapt DeepEvolves deep-research agent (Liu et al., 2025) and official implementation6 as retrieval-augmented baseline. Since candidate generation is already handled by our MolLEO architecture, we retain only DeepEvolves query-planning and web-search summarization components, injecting the resulting summaries into the design prompts. For each selected parent candidate (or pair), the planner generates = 4 queries based on the task objective, candidate(s) and oracle scores, evolutionary history, and top-N = 5 scoring candidates; the summarizer executes the queries and concatenates the results, with exclusive access to the search tool. We preserve the original prompt structure while replacing its generation-based progress signal with the fraction of the oracle-call budget consumed and retaining the 0.5 early/mature threshold. We reconstruct candidate ancestry chronologically and use the top-N candidates as (candidate, score) inspiration pairs. To limit information leakage, queries are restricted to general scientific principles rather than specific candidate solutions. The planner and summarizer use fixed models independent of the optimization backbone, while GPT-5-mini (Singh et al., 2025) is used as the optimization backbone, with all other optimizer hyperparameters matched to PRINCIPIA. WebSearch As web-based retrieval baseline, we use Google Search via the Serper API7. For each parent candidate (or parent pair) selected for an LLM operation, planner generates search query conditioned on the target property, task objective, parent candidate(s) and oracle scores, and current optimization progress. The query is issued to the search API, and the top-k retrieved passages are directly injected into the design prompt without LLM-based summarization. We adapt the queryplanning prompt from our DeepEvolve implementation by removing the evolutionary-history and inspiration blocks and instructing the planner to generate concise, keyword-style queries of 58 words for general scientific search. To align with PRINCIPIA, we fix the number of injected passages to 4, measure progress as the fraction of the oracle-call budget consumed, and use GPT-5-mini (Singh et al., 2025) as the fixed planner. The planner is constrained to retrieve general scientific principles rather than information about specific candidates to reduce potential information leakage and align with our research objectives (scientific principles), while all other optimization hyperparameters, including the initial population and population size, are matched to PRINCIPIA. C.2 MOLECULAR PROPERTY PREDICTION Direct Prediction The LLM predicts the molecular property from the task description and the query molecule represented as SMILES. The prompt specifies the required answer format without providing labeled examples or additional scientific knowledge. Few-Shot Prediction We provide {1, 3, 5, 7} labeled training molecules as examples for each query. Examples are selected by their Tanimoto similarity to the query using 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints with radius 2. Each example contains the molecular SMILES and its observed label, and the selected examples are included before the query in the prediction prompt. Internal Principles We augment the prediction prompt with fixed set of task-specific scientific principles generated by the internal knowledge of LLMs. These principles describe molecular characteristics and physicochemical factors relevant to the target property. The same principles are provided for every query within task and remain fixed throughout evaluation, without being updated from the observed training labels. External Principles We obtain task-specific scientific principles through web search. Given the task description, an LLM formulates search queries targeting general mechanisms, structure-activity relationships, and physicochemical determinants. We issue these queries through Google Search via the Serper API and collect result snippets together with page content from the top-ranked sources. An LLM then summarizes the retrieved material into predictive principles, with instructions to include only claims supported by the sources. Search queries target general domain knowledge and exclude specific query molecules, benchmark names, and lists of labeled compounds. The resulting principles are stored and provided as the same textual context for all query molecules within the task. Textual Summary We construct single textual summary by sequentially processing the batched training molecules. At each step, the LLM receives the task description, the previous summary, 6https://github.com/liugangcode/deepevolve.git 7https://serper.dev/

sections.title: E SUPPLEMENTARY EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Importance of Diversifying Learning Signals for Optimization In Table 6, we analyze different strategies for retrieving comparative causal hypotheses during scientific optimization. The results show that combining hypotheses associated with both increases and decreases in property fitness from reference to target leads to more effective discovery than exclusively retrieving hypotheses associated with either direction. This suggests that diversifying learning signals enables language models to learn from broader range of comparative evidence and associated hypotheses, thereby supporting the generation of more accurate comparative causal hypotheses and inductive principles aligned with the discovery objective, validating our design choice explained in Appendix Section A. Furthermore, retrieving hypotheses with consistently increasing or decreasing gains provides stronger learning signals than random retrieval, where informative signals may be diluted. Notably, PRINCIPIA consistently outperforms the plain optimization algorithm even when using diverse hypothesis retrieval strategies. This suggests that the comparative causal hypotheses and inductive principles constructed by PRINCIPIA remain useful across different retrieval strategies, supporting the overall quality of the constructed principles and the effectiveness of PRINCIPIA. Efficacy in Multi-Objective Discovery While we have demonstrated the effectiveness of PRINCIPIA across various discovery tasks, most involve single-objective optimization. To evaluate its robustness under diverse objectives, we consider multi-objective protein sequence engineering task that maximizes the Syn-3bfo fitness score, equivalent to the normalized negative Potts-model energy on the PDB 3bfo-derived synthetic landscape, while minimizing the Hamming distance from the wild-type sequence. Following Wang et al. (2025b), we scalarize the two objectives with equal weights. As shown in Figure 7, PRINCIPIA improves over the plain optimization algorithm, while other knowledge-augmented methods degrade over plain optimization algorithm, demonstrating the robustness of guidance from inductive principles constructed at test time across diverse discovery objectives. Analysis with Additional Metrics To further demonstrate the effectiveness of PRINCIPIA in accelerating scientific discovery through inductive principles constructed at test time, we evaluate its performance using additional metrics. In Table 7, we report the Hit Ratio after excluding essential genes from the ground-truth set, following the additional evaluation protocol adopted in Roohani et al. (2025). PRINCIPIA achieves the highest Hit Ratio on both the Scharenberg22 and IFNG gene perturbation tasks, outperforming the baseline optimization algorithms across both tasks. Furthermore, Figure 9 presents the Top-100 Average Score trends with respect to the number of oracle calls, complementary to the Top-10 AUC and Top-100 Average scores after fixed amount of oracle calls. The results show that PRINCIPIA consistently achieves higher Top-100 Average Scores than the existing optimization algorithms throughout the optimization process. These results provide further evidence that PRINCIPIA can effectively improve the performance of scientific discovery by constructing and applying task-specific inductive principles at test time.
